newsitem.title: MEXICO: INTERVIEW - Mexico cenbank head sees reserves limit.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Mexico cenbank head sees reserves limit.

text.p: The head of the Mexican central bank, Miguel Mancera, said the country's international reserves, which have soared this year, should not continue growing indefinitely.

"It's good to have more reserves, because it gives the security to foreign investors that there are enough resources to meet (debt) amortizations," Mancera, the governor of the Banco de Mexico, said in an interview late last week with Reuters.
"But reserves have an opportunity cost. They should not grow indefinitely."

Mexican net international reserves surged above $20 billion in late February for the first time since prior to Mexico's 1994-5 peso crisis, bouyed by purchases of dollars through "put" options that are regularly auctioned to the banks, revenue from state oil giant Petroleos Mexicanos, and Federal Government borrowing abroad.
Net foreign reserves on March 14 were $20.176 billion, up from $17.509 billion on Dec. 31, according to figures from the Banco de Mexico, which is Mexico's central bank.
Half of the current level, almost $10 billion, are in the form of loans from the International Monetary Fund, which Mexico has been paying back steadily.
Mancera said the central bank expects to pay some $3 billion to the IMF this year, which represent advance payments for $2.2 billion in addition to $800 million of scheduled amortizations.
Mexico has already announced prepayments of $1.5 billion in January and $590 million the following month.

Mancera declined to say what he considered an adequate level for hard currency stocks, but he said he had recently ordered a top Banco de Mexico economist to undertake a study of what the optimum level should be.
He cautioned, however: "There can hardly be a scientific answer".
He acknowledged that there was a trade-off between building reserves and promoting economic growth, and he indicated that at some stage the central bank may decide that it had accumulated enough.
At that point, he said, it could stop buying dollars through its at least once-a-month auctions of dollar "put" options. He declined to say when that was likely to be.
